subject: music
title: Post-punk (c. 1977–1984): after the first wave, bass, dub, and independent labels
dek: When the Sex Pistols split in January 1978, the short song did not stop. Groups in Manchester, Leeds, London, New York, Düsseldorf, and Tokyo kept independent 45s and changed the rhythm, the bass, and the studio. Critics later called the stretch post-punk.

thumb.alt: A curved red-brick apartment building on a Manchester street corner, with silver letters reading Hacienda apartments at ground level under a blue sky.

hero.alt: The curved red-brick Hacienda apartments on Whitworth Street West, Manchester, with the name in silver letters, a glass stair tower, and an older brick warehouse to the left.
hero.caption: The apartment block on the corner of Whitworth Street West and Albion Street, Manchester, photographed on 8 May 2018. Factory Records opened FAC 51 The Haçienda here on 21 May 1982. The club closed in 1997 and was demolished in 2002. The curved brick and the word Hacienda on this building are later. The address is the 1982 fact.

honesty: “Post-punk” is a press and critic label, not a union card and not a single sound. Writers applied it after the fact to records made roughly 1977–1984 that kept punk’s shortness and independent means and dropped its three-chord rulebook. This lesson is that first stretch. It is not a history of hardcore, which kept the shortness and raised the speed. It is not a synth-pop lesson: Human League’s Dare (1981) and the chart electronics that followed are named as a later fork, not taught. Gothic rock as a brand, industrial music as a separate catalogue, and the 1990s–2000s post-punk revival are out of scope. New York, Manchester, Leeds, Düsseldorf, and Tokyo were contemporaneous scenes, not a required pairing. 1970s and early-1980s band photographs are usually still in copyright, so the pictures here are buildings, a 1978 street outside Ratinger Hof, a museum chart, and a later bar interior, captioned as such. Where a free picture could not be found, the lesson does without. No AI people.

timeline.label: The hinge
timeline.detail: Wire issue Pink Flag in December: twenty-one short tracks that already leave first-wave punk’s grammar. In Manchester, Warsaw — Ian Curtis, Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook, Stephen Morris — are playing the same circuit that had watched the Sex Pistols at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in 1976. Pere Ubu in Cleveland record The Modern Dance. In Tokyo, Shinjuku Loft has been open since 1 October 1976.

timeline.label: After Winterland
timeline.detail: Sex Pistols’ last gig of the original run: Winterland, San Francisco, 14 January. The group splits. John Lydon forms Public Image Ltd in London with Keith Levene, Jah Wobble, and Jim Walker. “Public Image” (Virgin, 13 October); Public Image: First Issue (8 December). Magazine issue Real Life. Fast Product in Edinburgh issues Gang of Four’s Damaged Goods EP. Brian Eno compiles No New York. Factory Records puts out A Factory Sample (FAC 2) in December. From July, S-KEN runs Tokyo Rockers Sundays at his Roppongi studio.

timeline.label: The year of the LPs
timeline.detail: Joy Division, Unknown Pleasures (Factory FACT 10, 15 June), recorded at Strawberry Studios, Stockport, with Martin Hannett. The Slits, Cut (Island, September), produced by Dennis Bovell. Gang of Four, Entertainment! (EMI, 25 September). Talking Heads, Fear of Music (Sire). The Raincoats’ debut on Rough Trade. Public Image Ltd, Metal Box (Virgin, 23 November): three 12-inch 45s in a film canister. Cabaret Voltaire, Mix-Up. P-MODEL, In a Model Room (Warner Pioneer, August). Plastics record the tracks later heard on Welcome Back.

timeline.label: Curtis, Closer, New Order
timeline.detail: Ian Curtis dies by suicide on 18 May, aged 23, on the eve of Joy Division’s first North American tour. Closer (Factory FACT 25) appears on 18 July. “Love Will Tear Us Apart” (FAC 23) is already in the shops. The remaining members continue as New Order. Talking Heads issue Remain in Light (Sire, October). Friction issue their debut in Tokyo. PiL recut Metal Box as the gatefold Second Edition (22 February) after the canister pressing of about 60,000.

timeline.label: Machines, Hacienda, the window closes
timeline.detail: New Order’s “Ceremony” (FAC 33, March 1981). Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft issue Alles ist gut, recorded with Conny Plank; “Der Mussolini” is the single. The Birthday Party, from Melbourne, issue Prayers on Fire. Factory opens The Haçienda (FAC 51) on 21 May 1982. By 1983–84 the independent infrastructure is in place and several of these groups are already leaving the window: New Order toward dance records, Human League toward Dare, PiL toward This Is What You Want… This Is What You Get (1984). Hardcore and chart synth-pop are other forks. They are not this lesson.

fun_fact.title: The Unknown Pleasures sleeve is a radio plot of a pulsar, not a mountain range
fun_fact.text: Peter Saville designed the cover for Joy Division’s Unknown Pleasures in 1979 from a small diagram in the Cambridge Encyclopaedia of Astronomy. The image is a stack of successive radio pulses from CP1919, the first pulsar identified, later catalogued PSR B1919+21. Harold D. Craft Jr. plotted those pulses for his 1970 astronomy thesis, using data from the Arecibo Observatory; the encyclopaedia reprinted the figure. Saville reversed it to white lines on black and put no band name on the front. The chart photographed in this lesson is not that stacked plot. It is the 6 August 1967 paper printout, now shown at Cambridge, on which Jocelyn Bell Burnell marked the same object — “Pulsar CP 1919” — when the pulses were still a surprise. One pulsar, two graphics, ten years apart: a laboratory strip in 1967, a Factory sleeve in 1979.

sections.title: After Winterland, the short song was still useful

blocks.text: The Sex Pistols played their last concert of the original run at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on 14 January 1978, a Bill Graham hall far larger than CBGB or the 100 Club. John Lydon ended the night with a question — “Ever get the feeling you’ve been cheated?” — and left. The group split. That date ends one press story. It does not end the short song, the independent 45, or the cheap rehearsal space. What a lot of players refused next was not stadium rock, which the first wave had already shouted at. They refused the uniform that had followed: three chords as a rule, the tabloid face, the idea that the fight was over because the Pistols were over.

Some records had already walked out of that rulebook while the first wave was still in the shops. Wire’s Pink Flag, released in December 1977 on Harvest, holds twenty-one tracks, most of them brief, with stops and gaps where a chorus would have been. Pere Ubu, in Cleveland, issued The Modern Dance in early 1978: David Thomas’s voice, a synthesizer used as noise, songs that did not behave like a London 45. In Manchester, the group that had started as Warsaw after watching the Sex Pistols at the Lesser Free Trade Hall on 4 June 1976 were writing under a new name, Joy Division. None of this waited for a critic to invent a category. The category came later, in the weekly papers and then in books, and it stuck as “post-punk.”

The economics had not improved. Britain in 1978–81 was still a country of unemployment, closures, and, from 1979, a Conservative government under Margaret Thatcher. Manchester’s mills and docks were not a metaphor; they were a labour market. Leeds and Sheffield had the same weather in the figures. New York’s downtown rents were still low enough for a loft and a cheap PA. Those facts did not write the bass lines. They made the rehearsal time cheap, and they gave lyricists a vocabulary that did not have to be invented. Dub records from Jamaica — King Tubby, Lee “Scratch” Perry — were already in British shops and on John Peel’s radio show. Funk and disco were on the same radio, which is why a Leeds group could steal a rhythm without making a disco record. In Düsseldorf, NEU! and Can had spent the early 1970s putting repetition and a hard bass in the foreground. Those catalogues were on the shelf. Post-punk used them.

sections.title: London, Manchester, Leeds: three catalogues, not one committee

blocks.text: Do not start with a map that has one capital. London, Manchester, and Leeds made records in overlapping months. They shared independent shops, John Peel, and a few producers. They did not share a sound. The useful way through is three catalogues, then the labels that pressed them.

In London, Lydon formed Public Image Ltd in the summer of 1978 with Keith Levene on guitar, Jah Wobble (John Wardle) on bass, and Jim Walker on drums. The first single, “Public Image,” appeared on Virgin on 13 October 1978 and reached number nine on the UK Singles Chart. The debut album, Public Image: First Issue, followed on 8 December. The second album is the one to slow down for. Metal Box, released by Virgin on 23 November 1979, was three 12-inch records cut at 45 rpm and packed in an embossed metal film canister. Dennis Morris and the group took the idea from 16 mm film cans. Virgin did not want the cost; the group paid part of it from their advance. About 60,000 copies were pressed by the Metal Box Company. The set was deleted the day it appeared, then reissued on 22 February 1980 as Second Edition, a conventional gatefold. Wobble’s bass is the argument: long, dub-derived, in the front of the mix. Levene’s guitar is metallic and does not solo. Lydon’s voice sits on top without pretending to be Johnny Rotten. “Albatross,” “Poptones,” and “Careering” are the tracks that show the method. Death Disco, the 1979 single, put the same bass on a 45 that could be played in a club. This is not the Sex Pistols with extra effects. It is a different job.

In Manchester the label was the fact as much as the band. Tony Wilson, a presenter on Granada Television, and Alan Erasmus started Factory Records in 1978. Peter Saville designed the sleeves and treated each catalogue number — FAC 1, a poster; FAC 2, A Factory Sample, two 7-inches in December 1978 — as an object. Martin Hannett produced. Rob Gretton managed Joy Division and later sat on the board. The office, for a stretch, was a Victorian house at 86 Palatine Road, West Didsbury. Joy Division recorded Unknown Pleasures with Hannett at Strawberry Studios in Stockport over weekends in April 1979. Factory released it as FACT 10 on 15 June. Hook’s bass carries the tune; Morris’s drums are dry and delayed; Sumner’s guitar is a texture; Curtis sings as if the words were already a document. “Disorder” opens the album. “She’s Lost Control” and “New Dawn Fades” are the other tracks people name. Closer, recorded at Britannia Row in London in March 1980, appeared on 18 July as FACT 25, two months after Curtis’s death. “Love Will Tear Us Apart,” FAC 23, was already out. The remaining three members continued as New Order. Their first single, “Ceremony,” FAC 33, March 1981, is a Joy Division song finished after the fact. Factory later built a club: FAC 51 The Haçienda, designed by Ben Kelly, opened on 21 May 1982 at 11–13 Whitworth Street West, financed in large part by New Order and the label. ESG played the first night. That date sits at the edge of this lesson. The acid-house years of the Haçienda are another story.

blocks.alt: A red-brick Victorian house with a white arched doorway numbered 86, a two-storey bay window, and dark bargeboards, photographed from the front garden.
blocks.caption: 86 Palatine Road, West Didsbury, photographed on 10 August 2008. Factory Records used this house as its headquarters. The bay window and the number on the door are the building. The 1978–82 fact is the catalogue: FAC numbers, Joy Division, New Order, The Durutti Column, A Certain Ratio, and the later club on Whitworth Street West.

blocks.alt: A museum display of green grid paper with red ink traces, handwritten arrows, the date 6 AUG 1967, and the words Pulsar CP 1919, photographed behind glass.
blocks.caption: Chart examined by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, 6 August 1967, photographed in 2019 at Cambridge. The handwriting marks the first pulsar, CP1919. This is not Peter Saville’s Unknown Pleasures sleeve. Saville used a later stacked-pulse diagram of the same object, plotted by Harold D. Craft Jr. and printed in the Cambridge Encyclopaedia of Astronomy. The lesson keeps the laboratory sheet because it is a dated object of that pulsar, not because it is the record cover.

blocks.text: In Leeds, Gang of Four — Jon King, Andy Gill, Dave Allen, Hugo Burnham — treated funk as a political tool and guitar as something you chopped rather than soloed. Their first record was a 12-inch on Fast Product, the Edinburgh label run by Bob Last: Damaged Goods, with “Love Like Anthrax” and “Armalite Rifle,” late 1978. EMI signed them. Entertainment! appeared on 25 September 1979. “Damaged Goods,” “Natural’s Not In It,” “At Home He’s a Tourist,” and “Anthrax” are the tracks that show the method: Gill’s guitar cutting against Allen’s bass, King singing about work, sex, and slogans as if they were the same sentence. The BBC asked them to change “rubbers” to “rubbish” for Top of the Pops; they walked off. Around them in Leeds were the Mekons and Delta 5. None of this is Manchester exported down the M62. It is a university city with a small independent circuit and a group that had listened to Dr. Feelgood and to dub and had decided the riff should argue.

The rest of the British field is not a supporting cast. Howard Devoto left Buzzcocks and formed Magazine; Real Life appeared in 1978, and “Shot by Both Sides” is the 45. Siouxsie and the Banshees had played the 100 Club Punk Special in 1976; The Scream (1978) still has the first wave in its grain, and Kaleidoscope (1980) is already somewhere else. The Slits — Ari Up, Viv Albertine, Tessa Pollitt, with Palmolive on drums until she left, then Budgie — made Cut with Dennis Bovell in 1979: reggae timing, talk-singing, “Typical Girls” as a list that refuses the list. The Raincoats — Gina Birch, Ana da Silva — issued their debut on Rough Trade the same year. The Fall, with Mark E. Smith, were a Manchester group that did not join Factory’s design programme; Live at the Witch Trials is 1979, Hex Enduction Hour is 1982. Wire followed Pink Flag with Chairs Missing (1978) and 154 (1979). Geoff Travis’s Rough Trade had been a Notting Hill shop in 1976 and a label from 1978; it pressed the Raincoats and distributed a lot of the independent 45s that majors would not. Fast Product, Factory, Rough Trade, and, in New York, ZE Records (Michael Zilkha and Michel Esteban) are the catalogue names to keep, not a complete industry history.

sections.title: Bass in front, guitar at an angle, the studio as an instrument

blocks.text: A first-wave punk 45 is usually guitar, a count-in, and two minutes. A post-punk 45 often starts with the bass. Jah Wobble on Metal Box, Peter Hook on Unknown Pleasures, Dave Allen on Entertainment!, Tina Weymouth on Fear of Music: the low string carries the tune, and the guitar comments, chops, or leaves holes. That habit has a source in dub, where the bass and the drum are the track and the rest is dropped in and out. British players did not have to become reggae groups to learn it. They had to own the records and leave space. King Tubby and Lee Perry are influences here in the mix, not guest stars.

The guitar is often angular: a stuck rhythm, a metallic scrape, an anti-solo. Andy Gill said he wanted the opposite of a guitar hero. Keith Levene’s parts on Metal Box are sustained and sour. Bernard Sumner, on the Joy Division records, is closer to a keyboard that happens to be six strings. Drum machines and cheap synthesizers enter in these years without this lesson becoming a synthesizer history. Hannett used digital delay and a Marshall Time Modulator on Joy Division until the drums sounded like a room that did not exist. Cabaret Voltaire, in Sheffield, built pieces from tape at their Western Works studio. Human League’s first records, Reproduction (1979) and Travelogue (1980), are machine-led and still sit in this window; Dare (1981) is the chart fork that a later synth-pop lesson can take. DAF, in Düsseldorf, ran sequencers and a shout through Conny Plank’s studio and arrived at “Der Mussolini” in 1981. Funk and disco are borrowed as rhythm — Gang of Four, Talking Heads, James Chance and the Contortions — without the lesson turning into a disco survey. The point is a danceable 4/4 that does not apologise for remaining a guitar record, or a sequencer record that does not apologise for remaining loud.

Independent pressing and distribution did the unglamorous work. A Factory catalogue number, a Rough Trade bag, a Fast Product sleeve: these were how a Leeds or Manchester 45 reached a shop in London without waiting for EMI’s nerve to return. Majors still signed people — Virgin had PiL, EMI had Gang of Four, Island had the Slits, Sire had Talking Heads — so “independent” is a method, not a purity test. Peel’s radio show remained a national distributor that did not look like one. The sound is the bass and the gap. The business is a catalogue number and a van.

sections.title: The same years in New York, Düsseldorf, Tokyo, Melbourne

blocks.text: In New York the brief, named burst is No Wave. For five evenings in May 1978, Artists Space in Tribeca put on a series of downtown groups. Brian Eno compiled four of them — the Contortions, Teenage Jesus and the Jerks, Mars, DNA — on No New York, issued by Antilles in November 1978. James Chance (James Siegfried) ran the Contortions as a fight between funk and noise; “Contort Yourself” is the track that escaped the compilation. Lydia Lunch led Teenage Jesus. DNA were Arto Lindsay, Ikue Mori, and, for a stretch, Tim Wright, who had come from Pere Ubu. This is not CBGB’s 1975 circuit with a new haircut. It is shorter-lived, more art-world, and harsher. Talking Heads, who had used that earlier CBGB stage, continued as an art-school American parallel rather than a No Wave group: Fear of Music in 1979, with “I Zimbra” built on a Hugo Ball sound poem and African percussion, then Remain in Light in 1980 with Brian Eno. Pere Ubu, still in Cleveland, issued Dub Housing in November 1978. ZE Records in New York pressed some of the same downtown names and a lot of disco-not-disco that this lesson does not teach. The Pyramid Club opened in 1979 at 101 Avenue A; it is a later East Village address, useful as geography, not as a 1978 No Wave bill.

blocks.alt: A four-storey red-brick tenement at 101 Avenue A, New York, with a black fire escape, a yellow pyramid sign over a metal shutter, snow on the pavement, and a tailor’s awning to the left.
blocks.caption: 101 Avenue A, between East 6th and 7th Streets, photographed on 2 February 2011. The Pyramid Club opened here in 1979. The neo-Grec building dates from 1876. The snow, the Japanese restaurant sign, and the SUV are 2011. The 1978 No Wave series was at Artists Space in Tribeca, not at this door. The address is why the later club belongs in the same downtown years.
blocks.credit: Beyond My Ken / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: In West Germany the feeders were older than the word. NEU! and Can, from Düsseldorf and Cologne, had already put repetition, a dry drum, and a prominent bass on records in the early 1970s. The live address that mattered for the next generation in Düsseldorf was Ratinger Hof, a bar on Ratinger Straße. Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft — Gabi Delgado-López and Robert Görl, after an earlier larger line-up — took sequencers, a shout, and a Korg into Conny Plank’s studio outside Cologne and made Alles ist gut in 1981 for Virgin. “Der Mussolini” is a dance track built on a word Gabi liked the sound of; it is not a programme. Berlin’s SO36, on Oranienstraße in Kreuzberg, booked overlapping bills. Throbbing Gristle in London are industrial-adjacent in the same years; they are named so the border is visible, not so this becomes an industrial lesson.

blocks.alt: Black-and-white 1978 street scene: a brick bar with a Gothic Ratinger Hof sign, beer advertisements, a pale car at the kerb, flyposters, and a handful of people on the pavement.
blocks.caption: Ratinger Hof, Düsseldorf, 20 May 1978, photographed by Ralf Zeigermann. The Gothic sign, the Düssel-Alt boards, the flyposters, and the car are 1978. DAF and the Düsseldorf groups used this bar. The people on the pavement are not identified here; they are the street, not a band portrait.
blocks.credit: Ralf Zeigermann / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.text: In Tokyo the calendar overlaps rather than copies. Shinjuku Loft opened on 1 October 1976. From July 1978, S-KEN ran Sunday concerts at his Roppongi studio under the name Tokyo Rockers — Friction, Lizard, Mirrors among them. Reck, Friction’s bassist, had already played in New York with Teenage Jesus and the Jerks and then come back; that is a person on two bills, not a theory of influence. Plastics — Toshio Nakanishi, Chica Sato, Hajime Tachibana — made clipped, humorous electronic pop; “Top Secret Man” and “Copy” are the tracks that travelled, and Welcome Back (1980) is the album that carried them into Island’s American shops. P-MODEL, led by Susumu Hirasawa, issued In a Model Room on Warner Pioneer in August 1979; “Art Mania” (“Bijutsukan de atta hito daro”) is the single. Hikashu were in the same Tokyo years. None of this is an assigned Asian verse. It is a city with live houses, imported 45s, and groups who had their own jokes and machines.

blocks.alt: A dark bar interior: liquor bottles on shelves, a round clock with a purple neon ring reading American Original Watch Made in New York, and a small Japanese sign refusing alcohol sales to minors.
blocks.caption: The bar at Shinjuku Loft, photographed on 19 June 2007. Shinjuku Loft opened on 1 October 1976 in Nishi-Shinjuku and moved to Kabuki-chō on 1 April 1999 after a dispute with the old building’s owner. This is the later bar, not a 1978 stage shot. The live house is why it is here; the neon clock is 2007.

blocks.text: In Australia the Saints and Radio Birdman had already made first-wave records; they belong to the earlier capsule. The group that sits in this window is the Birthday Party, from Melbourne — Nick Cave, Rowland S. Howard, Mick Harvey, Tracy Pew, Phill Calvert — who moved to London and issued Prayers on Fire in 1981 and Junkyard in 1982. That is a contemporaneous Australian line into the same British independent shops, not a ranking of cities.

sections.title: What the years left: a catalogue, a club, and other forks

blocks.text: By 1984 the first stretch is over as a scene, even if several of the groups are still together. What it left is easier to name than a sound. Independent labels with catalogue numbers, a distribution habit (Rough Trade’s network, Factory’s self-image as a design project), and a British and American press that now had the word “post-punk” to file records under. New Order took the Joy Division remainder into dance singles and, with Factory, into the Haçienda; the acid-house period of that club is after this lesson. Human League’s Dare and the chart synthesizer hits of 1981–84 are a fork this capsule refuses to teach. Hardcore, especially in the United States, kept punk’s shortness and raised the speed; it is the other after. Gothic rock as a shop tag took Siouxsie, early Cure, and the Joy Division bass and made a costume. Industrial music kept Throbbing Gristle’s and Cabaret Voltaire’s tape and noise and built another catalogue. The 1990s and 2000s revival — groups filing themselves as post-punk — is out of scope. The 1977–84 fact is smaller: a few cities, a few dozen records, bass in the front, and a critic’s word that arrived on time to name them.
If the first wave’s refusal was a two-minute song in a small venue, what is being refused once the bass, the dub drop, and an independent catalogue number are doing the work?

glossary.explain: Press and critic label, applied after the fact, for records made roughly 1977–1984 that kept punk’s shortness and independent means and dropped its three-chord rulebook. Not a single sound or committee.
The first-wave short, loud guitar music of c. 1974–78, associated with CBGB, the 100 Club, and independent 45s. This lesson starts after that wave’s burnout. See the earlier capsule.
A later, faster punk that kept the shortness and raised the speed. Named here as another fork after 1978, not taught.
Chart electronics of the early 1980s, associated here with Human League’s Dare (1981). Named as a later fork, not this lesson.
Radio and press name that tried to separate pop and art-school groups from “punk.” Talking Heads were filed both ways. In this lesson they are an American art-school parallel, not a radio format.

Brief New York downtown burst, 1978, associated with the Artists Space series and the compilation No New York (Contortions, Teenage Jesus and the Jerks, Mars, DNA). Harsher and shorter-lived than CBGB’s mid-1970s circuit.
Later shop and press tag that took Siouxsie, early Cure, and the Joy Division bass and made a costume. Named as an after, not taught.
Separate catalogue around Throbbing Gristle, and parts of Cabaret Voltaire’s tape work. Named so the border is visible, not taught as a history.
Jamaican studio practice: bass and drums as the track, other parts dropped in and out, associated here with King Tubby and Lee Perry as an influence on PiL and on British independent records.
American dance rhythm borrowed by Gang of Four, Talking Heads, and the Contortions. In this lesson it is a rhythm source, not a genre survey.
Late-1970s dance music. Post-punk borrowed its 4/4 and bass without this lesson becoming a disco history.
Loose British press name for early-1970s West German groups including NEU! and Can. Feeders for some post-punk repetition and bass, not the same movement.

Manchester independent label, 1978–92, started by Tony Wilson and Alan Erasmus. Joy Division, New Order, The Durutti Column, A Certain Ratio. Catalogue numbers prefixed FAC or FACT. Later opened the Haçienda.
Factory’s numbering of posters, records, and the club (FAC 51). A design habit as much as a filing system.
Notting Hill record shop from 1976 (Geoff Travis) and a label from 1978. Pressed the Raincoats and distributed many independent 45s. Shop and label later split.

New York label run by Michael Zilkha and Michel Esteban. Downtown and disco-not-disco catalogue in the same years.
British label that signed Public Image Ltd and, later, DAF. A major relative to Factory, still the PiL catalogue.

Label that issued Talking Heads, including Fear of Music and Remain in Light.
Label that issued the No New York compilation, November 1978.

PiL’s second album, Virgin, 23 November 1979. Three 12-inch 45 rpm discs in an embossed metal film canister; about 60,000 copies. Later reissued as Second Edition.
Gatefold reissue of Metal Box, 22 February 1980, after the canister pressing was deleted.
Manufacturer of the film-canister packaging for Metal Box.
Opening track of Metal Box: long, bass-forward, about ten minutes. The listen link in this lesson is the Second Edition master.
Metal Box track. One of the three usually named with Albatross and Careering to show PiL’s 1979 method.
Metal Box track.
PiL single, 1979. The same bass method on a 45; related to the Metal Box track issued as “Swan Lake.”

glossary.term: This Is What You Want… This Is What You Get
glossary.explain: PiL album, 1984. Named as the edge of this lesson’s window, not taught.

Salford/Manchester group: Ian Curtis, Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook, Stephen Morris. Began as Warsaw. Unknown Pleasures (1979), Closer (1980). Ended with Curtis’s death; the others continued as New Order.
Joy Division’s earlier name, 1977–78, taken after they watched the Sex Pistols at the Lesser Free Trade Hall.
Joy Division singer and lyricist. Died by suicide, 18 May 1980, aged 23, on the eve of the group’s first North American tour.
Joy Division guitarist; later New Order singer, guitarist, and synthesizer player.
Joy Division and New Order bassist. The high, melodic bass on Unknown Pleasures.
Joy Division and New Order drummer.
Joy Division’s debut album, Factory FACT 10, 15 June 1979. Recorded at Strawberry Studios, Stockport, with Martin Hannett. Sleeve by Peter Saville from a CP1919 pulsar plot.
Joy Division’s second album, Factory FACT 25, 18 July 1980. Recorded at Britannia Row, London, in March 1980. Issued after Curtis’s death.
Opening track of Unknown Pleasures. The listen link is the 2007 remaster.
Unknown Pleasures track.
Unknown Pleasures track.
Joy Division single, Factory FAC 23, 1980.
Joy Division’s self-released 1978 EP, before the Factory albums.
Factory’s early release, December 1978: two 7-inches including Joy Division’s “Digital” and “Glass,” plus The Durutti Column, Cabaret Voltaire, and John Dowie.
Joy Division track on A Factory Sample.
Joy Division track on A Factory Sample.
Group formed by Sumner, Hook, and Morris after Curtis’s death, 1980. First single “Ceremony,” FAC 33, March 1981. Later financed the Haçienda with Factory.
New Order’s first single, FAC 33, March 1981. A Joy Division song finished after Curtis’s death.
Factory’s club at 11–13 Whitworth Street West, Manchester. Opened 21 May 1982; closed 1997; demolished 2002. ESG played the first night. The acid-house years are after this lesson.
Manchester streets at the Haçienda’s corner, near Castlefield.
Victorian house in West Didsbury used as Factory Records’ headquarters.
Recording studio in Stockport. Unknown Pleasures was recorded there, April 1979.
London studio where Closer was recorded, March 1980.
Manchester hall. Sex Pistols played there on 4 June 1976; members of the future Joy Division were in the audience. A punk date, named here as origin only.
Factory group, Vini Reilly. On A Factory Sample; The Return of the Durutti Column (1980) was issued in a sandpaper sleeve.

glossary.term: The Return of the Durutti Column
glossary.explain: Factory album, 1980, sandpaper sleeve. The sandpaper idea had been discussed around Metal Box and landed here instead.
Factory group, Manchester, funk-leaning, contemporaneous with Joy Division on the same label.
Bronx group. Played the Haçienda’s opening night, 21 May 1982.
Comedian/musician on A Factory Sample.
The first pulsar identified, discovered in 1967. Stacked pulses of this object, plotted by Harold D. Craft Jr., became the Unknown Pleasures sleeve.
Astronomer who, in 1967 at Cambridge, recognised the pulsed radio signal later named CP1919. The museum chart in this lesson is her printout, not Saville’s sleeve.
Astronomer. Plotted successive CP1919 pulses for his 1970 thesis; the Cambridge Encyclopaedia of Astronomy reprinted the figure Saville used.
Radio observatory in Puerto Rico. Source of the pulsar data Craft plotted.
Book from which Peter Saville took the stacked-pulse diagram for Unknown Pleasures.
Leeds group: Jon King, Andy Gill, Dave Allen, Hugo Burnham. Damaged Goods EP (Fast Product, 1978); Entertainment! (EMI, 1979).
Gang of Four singer and lyricist.
Gang of Four guitarist. Chopped, anti-hero guitar on Entertainment!.
Gang of Four bassist on Entertainment!.
Gang of Four drummer on Entertainment!.
Gang of Four’s debut album, EMI, 25 September 1979.
Gang of Four song. Fast Product EP, 1978; remade on Entertainment!, 1979. The listen link is the album version.
Gang of Four track on the Fast Product EP and on Entertainment!.
Gang of Four track on the Fast Product EP.
Entertainment! track.
Gang of Four single, 1979. The BBC asked them to change “rubbers” to “rubbish” for Top of the Pops; they walked off.
Leeds group, contemporaneous with Gang of Four.
Leeds group, contemporaneous with Gang of Four.
Canvey Island pub-rock group. Andy Gill cited Wilko Johnson’s guitar as a model. A feeder, not post-punk.
Left Buzzcocks and formed Magazine. Real Life, 1978.
Howard Devoto’s group after Buzzcocks. Real Life (1978); “Shot by Both Sides.”
Magazine’s debut album, 1978.
Magazine single, 1978.
Manchester first-wave group. Named here because Devoto left them for Magazine. Taught in the punk capsule.
London group. Played the 100 Club Punk Special in 1976. The Scream (1978); Kaleidoscope (1980) marks the shift this lesson cares about.
Singer, Siouxsie and the Banshees.
Siouxsie and the Banshees’ debut album, 1978. Still close to the first wave.
Siouxsie and the Banshees album, 1980. Already somewhere else.
London group: Ari Up, Viv Albertine, Tessa Pollitt; Palmolive then Budgie on drums. Cut (Island, 1979), produced by Dennis Bovell.
Singer, the Slits. Also sang backing vocals on Talking Heads’ “I Zimbra.”
Guitarist, the Slits.
Bassist, the Slits.
Early Slits drummer; left before Cut was finished.
Drummer on the Slits’ Cut after Palmolive left; later in Siouxsie and the Banshees.
The Slits’ debut album, Island, September 1979, produced by Dennis Bovell.
Track on Cut. The listen link is the Island studio version.
Dub producer. Produced the Slits’ Cut.
London group, Gina Birch and Ana da Silva. Debut album on Rough Trade, 1979.
The Raincoats, bass and vocals.
The Raincoats, guitar and vocals.
Manchester group, Mark E. Smith. Live at the Witch Trials (1979); Hex Enduction Hour (1982). Not a Factory design project.
Singer and lyricist of the Fall.
The Fall’s debut album, 1979. Studio record, despite the title.
The Fall album, 1982.
London group. Pink Flag (December 1977) sits on the hinge out of first-wave punk; Chairs Missing (1978) and 154 (1979) are already in this lesson’s window.
Wire album, Harvest, December 1977. Twenty-one short tracks. The hinge named in the punk capsule as an after; taught here as a start.
Wire album, 1978.
Wire album, 1979.
New York group: David Byrne, Tina Weymouth, Chris Frantz, Jerry Harrison. CBGB in the first wave; Fear of Music (1979) and Remain in Light (1980) are the records this lesson slows down for.
Talking Heads singer and guitarist.
Talking Heads bassist.
Talking Heads drummer.
Talking Heads keyboardist and guitarist.
Producer of Talking Heads’ Fear of Music and Remain in Light; compiler of No New York.
Talking Heads album, Sire, 1979, produced by Brian Eno. Opens with “I Zimbra.”
Fear of Music track, also a 1980 single. Hugo Ball’s sound poem Gadji beri bimba set over African percussion. The listen link is the 2005 remaster.
Talking Heads album, Sire, October 1980, produced with Brian Eno. Named as the American art-school continuation, not a No Wave record.
Dada poet. His sound poem Gadji beri bimba is the lyric source of “I Zimbra.”
Hugo Ball sound poem adapted as the lyric of Talking Heads’ “I Zimbra.”
Cleveland group, David Thomas. The Modern Dance (early 1978); Dub Housing (November 1978). Contemporaneous with British post-punk, not a copy of it.
Singer, Pere Ubu.
Pere Ubu album, early 1978.
Pere Ubu album, November 1978.
Bassist. Pere Ubu, then DNA in New York.
Tribeca gallery. Staged the May 1978 No Wave concert series.
Compilation produced by Brian Eno, Antilles, November 1978: Contortions, Teenage Jesus and the Jerks, Mars, DNA.
No Wave group led by James Chance. On No New York; “Contort Yourself” is the track that travelled.
Singer and saxophonist, the Contortions; also recorded as James White and the Blacks.
Contortions track, the No Wave song that most often leaves the compilation.
No Wave group led by Lydia Lunch. Reck from Tokyo played bass with them before returning to form Friction.
Singer, Teenage Jesus and the Jerks.
No Wave group. On No New York.
No Wave group: Arto Lindsay, Ikue Mori, and for a stretch Tim Wright. On No New York.
Guitarist and singer, DNA.
Drummer, DNA.
Club at 101 Avenue A, East Village, opened 1979. A later downtown address; not the 1978 Artists Space series. The photograph is 2011.
315 Bowery. First-wave New York club. Named here as the earlier stage Talking Heads left from, not retaught.
Sheffield group. Tape and machines at Western Works. Mix-Up (1979). Also on A Factory Sample.
Cabaret Voltaire album, 1979.
Cabaret Voltaire’s Sheffield studio.
Sheffield group. Reproduction (1979) and Travelogue (1980) sit in this window; Dare (1981) is the synth-pop fork named as out of scope.
Human League album, 1979.
Human League album, 1980.
Human League album, 1981. Chart synthesizer pop; out of scope for this lesson.
Düsseldorf group, early 1970s. Repetition and a hard drum as a feeder for later German and British records.
Cologne group, late 1960s–70s. Bass, repetition, studio as instrument. A feeder, not a post-punk band.
Bar on Ratinger Straße, Düsseldorf. Live address for the late-1970s Düsseldorf groups, including DAF. The photograph is 20 May 1978.
Club on Oranienstraße, Kreuzberg, Berlin. Booked overlapping new-wave and post-punk bills in these years.
Düsseldorf duo of Gabi Delgado-López and Robert Görl (after an earlier larger line-up). Alles ist gut (1981), with Conny Plank; “Der Mussolini.”
DAF singer.
DAF drummer and sequencer player.
German producer. Recorded DAF’s Alles ist gut; earlier records with NEU! and others.
DAF album, Virgin, 1981. The listen link is Groenland’s later official reissue of that studio album.
DAF track and single from Alles ist gut, 1981.
London group, industrial-adjacent in these years. Named as a border, not taught.
Tokyo live house, opened 1 October 1976 in Nishi-Shinjuku; moved to Kabuki-chō on 1 April 1999. The bar photograph is 2007 at the later site.
Tokyo musician and promoter. Ran Tokyo Rockers Sundays at his Roppongi studio from July 1978.
Name of the 1978 Roppongi Sunday gigs and of the groups around them (Friction, Lizard, Mirrors).
Tokyo group. Reck and Chiko Hige; debut album 1980. Reck had played with Teenage Jesus in New York.
Bassist. Teenage Jesus and the Jerks in New York, then Friction in Tokyo. A person on two bills.
Tokyo Rockers group.
Tokyo Rockers group.
Tokyo group: Toshio Nakanishi, Chica Sato, Hajime Tachibana. “Top Secret Man,” “Copy”; Welcome Back (1980).
Plastics, guitar and ideas.
Plastics, vocals.
Plastics, guitar.
Plastics track, widely issued on Welcome Back (1980). The listen link is JVCKENWOOD Victor’s 2018 digital issue.
Plastics track from the same years as “Top Secret Man.”
Plastics album, 1980, which carried their tracks into Island’s American shops.
Tokyo group led by Susumu Hirasawa. In a Model Room (Warner Pioneer, August 1979); “Art Mania.”
Singer and guitarist, P-MODEL.
P-MODEL debut album, Warner Pioneer, August 1979.
P-MODEL single from In a Model Room, 1979.
aliases: 美術館で会った人だろ

glossary.explain: Tokyo group, late 1970s–early 1980s, contemporaneous with Plastics and P-MODEL.
Melbourne group — Nick Cave, Rowland S. Howard, Mick Harvey, Tracy Pew, Phill Calvert — who moved to London. Prayers on Fire (1981), Junkyard (1982).
Singer, the Birthday Party.
Guitarist, the Birthday Party.
The Birthday Party.
Bassist, the Birthday Party.
Drummer, the Birthday Party.
The Birthday Party album, 1981.
The Birthday Party album, 1982.
Brisbane first-wave group. Named as already taught in the punk capsule.
Sydney first-wave group. Named as already taught in the punk capsule.
Jamaican dub engineer. Named as an influence on how British post-punk used bass and space.
Jamaican producer. Named with King Tubby as a dub source, not as a guest on these records.
American promoter. Winterland was his San Francisco hall.
San Francisco hall. Sex Pistols’ last gig of the original run, 14 January 1978.
100 Oxford Street, London. Punk Special, 1976. Named as the earlier stage Siouxsie left from.
Label that issued Wire’s Pink Flag, 1977.
Post-war radical group. A slogan from Ivan Chtcheglov, “The Hacienda Must Be Built,” gave Factory’s club its name.
Wrote Formulary for a New Urbanism, source of the Haçienda’s name.
Mid-to-late 1960s studios and longer songs. The earlier music capsule. Named so the sequence of lessons is visible.
1964 press name for British beat groups on the US charts. Two music capsules earlier. Not taught again here.
